title: Sagano: A Sound the State Decided to Protect
description: The Arashiyama bamboo grove is one of the few places on Earth listed by a government for what it sounds like, not what it looks like. In 1996 Japan's Environment Agency added its wind-through-moso rustle to the official 100 Soundscapes of Japan.
alignmentNote: Pure — a place and a soundscape tradition; scholarly meaning-making core.

verifiedFacts.fact: In 1996, Japan's Ministry of the Environment (then Environment Agency) designated the Sagano/Arashiyama bamboo grove's sound as one of the 100 Soundscapes of Japan.
The 100 Soundscapes were chosen from 738 public submissions by the Japan Soundscape Study Group.
The project was framed as a response to noise pollution and a way to preserve the country's characteristic sounds.
The grove consists mostly of moso bamboo, Phyllostachys edulis.
Moso bamboo has been measured growing up to 114.5 centimeters per day, more than a meter.

sources.name: PMC: Rapid growth of Moso bamboo

verifiedFacts.fact: The main path through the grove is roughly 500 meters long and about 140 meters wide, running between Tenryu-ji and Nonomiya shrine.
Tenryu-ji was founded in 1339 by the shogun Ashikaga Takauji.

The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter (Taketori Monogatari) is considered the oldest surviving Japanese monogatari, dating to the late 9th or early 10th century, and opens with a bamboo cutter finding a tiny girl inside a stalk of bamboo.

sources.name: TV Tropes summary citing standard sources

verifiedFacts.fact: Other entries on the 100 Soundscapes list include the Ise-Shima ama divers' whistled breathing (isobue) and various temple bells and foghorns.
Heian-period aristocrats kept retreats in the Arashiyama district (794–1185).

primarySources.name: PMC peer-reviewed paper on Moso bamboo growth rate
arashiyamabamboogrove.org (informational site, used as lead, verified against others)

contestedPoints.claim: Whether the grove is a natural forest or a planted/managed plantation dating to the Heian period.
contestedPoints.handling: Caption avoids the question entirely. It says only that Heian aristocrats kept retreats in the district, which is uncontested. The Wikipedia article calls it a 'natural bamboo forest' while some sources describe long-standing cultivation; we do not adjudicate this.

contestedPoints.claim: Exact authorship for the 1996 designation is sometimes given as 'Ministry of the Environment' and sometimes as the predecessor 'Environment Agency.'
contestedPoints.handling: Caption uses 'Japanese government' in the lead and clarifies 'then the Environment Agency' in the paragraph about the list, which matches Grokipedia/Wikipedia framing of the agency's later renaming.

caption.draft:
In 1996 the Japanese government catalogued one hundred sounds it wanted future generations to be able to hear. Temple bells in Kyoto. Foghorns off Hokkaido. The whistled breath of the Ise-Shima ama divers surfacing for air. And, in Arashiyama on the western edge of Kyoto, the noise a five hundred meter corridor of moso bamboo makes when the wind moves through it.

The grove itself is not large. The path runs about half a kilometer between Tenryu-ji, the Zen temple founded in 1339 by the shogun Ashikaga Takauji, and the smaller Nonomiya shrine. The stalks above it are Phyllostachys edulis, the species that during its growing weeks can lengthen by more than a meter in a single day. Heian aristocrats kept retreats here a thousand years ago. The oldest surviving Japanese narrative, the Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, opens with a man finding a child inside one of these stalks.

The 1996 list was assembled from 738 public nominations by something called the Japan Soundscape Study Group, working under what was then the Environment Agency. The stated reason was noise pollution. Rather than legislate against the new sounds, the agency chose to name and protect the old ones. The grove was registered for its rustle and creak, the dry knocking of culms against culms, the way leaves fifty meters overhead behave like a long instrument the weather plays.

A culture that decides a sound is worth preserving has already decided that listening is.

titleOverImage.text: A sound the state decided to protect

title: The bronze lump that turned out to be a 2,000-year-old computer
description: The Antikythera mechanism: a corroded shoebox of Greek bronze gears, pulled from a 1st-century BC shipwreck in 1900, that modeled the sky.
alignmentNote: Pure — an ancient frontier technology that reopens an old question; academic depth.

verifiedFacts.fact: The Antikythera wreck was discovered by sponge divers from Symi in 1900 and salvaged with the Hellenic Royal Navy in 1900-1901.
Greek archaeologist Valerios Stais identified a gear wheel in the corroded lump on 17 May 1902 in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

sources.name: DPMA (German Patent and Trade Mark Office)

verifiedFacts.fact: The mechanism is now split into 82 fragments, with about a third of the original surviving, including 30 corroded bronze gearwheels.

sources.name: Freeth et al. 2021, Scientific Reports, via UCL Discovery

verifiedFacts.fact: The wooden case was approximately 34 cm x 18 cm x 9 cm; the largest gear is about 13 cm in diameter and originally had 223 teeth.
The mechanism predicted solar and lunar eclipses, tracked positions of sun and moon, and displayed the cycle of the Panhellenic games.

sources.name: Nature Astronomy: Our current knowledge of the Antikythera Mechanism

verifiedFacts.fact: In 2005, microfocus X-ray Computed Tomography decoded inscriptions and gear teeth inside the fragments.
The 2021 UCL Antikythera Research Team model, led by Tony Freeth, reconstructs a planetary 'Cosmos' on the front display, with Venus modeled on a 462-year period using a 63-tooth gear.

sources.name: Freeth et al. 2021, Scientific Reports (UCL Discovery)

verifiedFacts.fact: The mechanism is generally dated to the 2nd-1st century BCE; eclipse-prediction analyses (Carman & Evans 2014; Freeth 2014) point to dates in the range 205-187 BCE for the inscribed eclipses.
Nothing of comparable mechanical complexity is known to survive for roughly the next 1,400 years.

primarySources.name: Freeth, T. et al. (2021). A Model of the Cosmos in the ancient Greek Antikythera Mechanism. Scientific Reports.
Freeth, T. & Jones, A. (2012). The Cosmos in the Antikythera Mechanism. ISAW Papers / Nature Astronomy review (2017).

contestedPoints.claim: Exact construction date of the mechanism
contestedPoints.handling: Caption gives the broad 'first century BC' frame consistent with the wreck and avoids picking sides between the 150-100 BC and 205 BC schools.

contestedPoints.claim: Original total gear count (37+ proposed in some reconstructions vs. 30 surviving)
contestedPoints.handling: Caption states only the surviving count of 30 gears, which is uncontested.
Caption hedges with 'roughly' and 'is known to survive' rather than asserting absolute uniqueness.

caption.draft:
In 1900, sponge divers from the island of Symi, working in fifty meters of water off Antikythera, surfaced with a bronze arm. The wreck below was a Roman cargo ship that had gone down in the first century BC, hauling statues and amphorae. Among the haul that reached the National Archaeological Museum in Athens was an unremarkable corroded lump. It sat in a drawer. In May 1902, the archaeologist Valerios Stais noticed a gear wheel embedded in the bronze.

What he had found is now split into 82 fragments, only about a third of the original. Inside the surviving pieces are thirty hand-cut bronze gears, the largest about 13 centimeters across with 223 teeth. The whole device once lived inside a wooden case roughly the size of a shoebox, around 34 by 18 by 9 centimeters, turned by a hand crank. Microfocus X-ray CT scanning in 2005 read the inscriptions and the gear teeth through the corrosion. The machine predicted solar and lunar eclipses, tracked the position of the sun and moon, and counted out the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games.

In 2021 a team at UCL, led by Tony Freeth, published a model of the front face: a mechanical cosmos with the planets stepping forward in their correct ancient ratios, Venus tied to a 462-year period through a 63-tooth gear. Nothing of comparable mechanical complexity is known to survive for roughly the next fourteen hundred years. The strangest part is not that the Greeks built it. The strangest part is that it sat in a museum drawer, unread, for a year, while everyone admired the statues.

titleOverImage.text: A bronze cosmos, the size of a shoebox
